title: Association between perceived indoor environmental characteristics and occupants' mental well-being, cognitive performance, productivity, satisfaction in workplaces: A systematic review
review_question: To systematically review the effects of perceived indoor environmental characteristics (PIEC) on occupants' mental well-being, cognitive performance, productivity, and satisfaction in workplaces.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included studies focused on adult office workers in normal or mock-up office environments, investigating at least one perceived indoor environmental characteristic (PIEC) and at least one outcome (mental well-being, cognitive performance, productivity, satisfaction). Excluded studies on home/flexible/outdoor/non-office workplaces, environmental chambers, virtual offices, unclear interventions, special devices, outcomes measured by unvalidated instruments, physiological health only, sick building syndrome symptoms, study protocols, systematic reviews, qualitative studies, or non-peer reviewed publications. Only peer-reviewed journals published after 1980 in English were included.

synthesis_conclusions: Effects of indoor climate, space & furniture & privacy, and visual quality of naturalness were broadly studied, while visual quality of decoration and environmental maintenance received less attention.
Many studies supported significant positive effects of indoor climate, space & furniture & privacy, and visual quality of naturalness on mental well-being, productivity, and satisfaction.
There is a clear lack of consistency in the studies of cognitive performance across all five environmental factors.
New studies are required to identify effects of visual quality of decoration and environmental maintenance on occupants.
Experimental studies (randomized controlled and quasi) are necessary to test the association between these environmental factors and occupants' performances in offices.
evidence_gaps: Lack of studies on effects of visual quality of decoration and environmental maintenance on occupants.
Inconsistency in findings regarding the impact of environmental factors on cognitive performance.
Need for more experimental studies (randomized controlled and quasi-experimental trials) to test associations in real office environments.
Further investigation needed on the mediating effect of visual properties (e.g., coherence, prospect) of natural elements on mental well-being and work performances.
Need for more detailed design analyses of naturalness, including amount, distributions, and configurations of natural elements.
Need for more opportunities to adjust layout, workstation, and furniture to improve perceived privacy.
Further investigation into the characteristics of office interior components (e.g., number, distribution, size, shape) on mental and work performances.
More investigations on the effect of space, furniture, and privacy on occupants' cognition.
More studies on effects of visual features of workstation (e.g., texture, colour, material).
Unclear relationship between air quality and employees' cognitive performance.
Unclear relationship between workplace cleanliness and cognitive performance/productivity.
Lack of experiments (controlled intervention studies) for environmental maintenance.
No clear evidence to prove the combined effect of environmental factors on occupants' cognitive performance.
Need for more investigations to clarify the importance rank of five environmental factors on occupants' mental well-being, cognition, and productivity.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Methodological quality of 55 eligible articles was assessed using the U.S. National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool. Overall study quality was assessed as 'good', 'fair', or 'poor'. Most studies were rated as 'fair' quality. Observational studies (n=38) generally used clear measures and reported valid outcomes, but most lacked sample size justification and blinding of outcome assessors. Cohort studies (n=8) had sufficient timeframe and assessed interventions prior to outcomes, but only 7 controlled confounders. Cross-sectional studies (n=30) did not report confounder analysis. Controlled intervention studies (n=13) adopted proper experimental settings but most lacked sample size analysis, randomization methods, and blinding. Before-after studies (n=4) had clear questions and measures but lacked blinding and some had low follow-up rates.
heterogeneity_sources: Inconsistencies in findings across different studies for certain outcomes (e.g., natural elements and mental well-being indicators like stress, anxiety, emotional well-being, work engagement; natural elements and attention; temperature and mental workload/productivity/satisfaction).
Variations in study design (cross-sectional vs. experimental), sample size, and specific measures used across studies.

limitations: Potential biases due to sample size setting, with many studies lacking clear justification for sample size, potentially reducing generalizability.
Over half of studies used cross-sectional surveys and self-reported questionnaires, which may not provide strong evidence for causal effects.
Controlled intervention experiments and longitudinal studies mainly explored conventional environmental characteristics, with less attention to decoration, naturalness, and perceived privacy.
Exclusion of articles in non-English languages and grey literature.
Potential for overlooked critical search terms in the search syntax.
Possible biases during the review process despite strict protocol.
Overall 'fair' quality of included studies suggests remaining biases that could influence generalization and transferability.
